The core insight of [1447] lies in contrasting two rating systems: USAU’s ad hoc, sine-weighted iterative approach versus a clean least-squares formulation. The LS system, defined by r̂ = (ATA)⁻¹ATb, directly maps match outcomes to team strengths in a linear fashion, offering interpretability and scalability. Its key innovation is the use of score-cap normalization, which rescales differentials to a fixed cap (e.g., 15) to mitigate distortions from variable scoring rules. This normalization ensures that a 12-8 game is treated equivalently to a 15-10 game in terms of strength signal. In contrast, USAU’s method introduces nonlinearity via a sine function modulating the margin-of-victory, which complicates interpretation and requires manual calibration. The empirical finding that LS outperforms USAU suggests that simpler, principled models may dominate complex heuristics in structured domains like ultimate frisbee. The failure mode of LS occurs when the schedule matrix lacks sufficient connectivity or when the system is underdetermined. For GSE, this implies leveraging LS as a stable baseline while allowing more flexible models to refine predictions. The dual nature of LS—both as a static kernel and a dynamic input—enables it to support both Bayesian inference and state-transition logic in GSE.
